title: Liquidity services and asset returns
prompt: Two riskless one-period assets have identical terminal payoffs. Only asset A can settle an intermediate purchase. Holding A has no additional cost, investors can freely choose either asset, and B supplies no other advantage. Which proposed equilibrium requires an additional friction?
correct: Asset B trades at a strictly higher purchase price than A.
wrong: A and B trade at the same price when settlement liquidity is abundant.
A trades at a higher price when its settlement service is scarce.
An investor with no settlement need is indifferent at equal prices.
explanation: A weakly dominates B in services with the same payoff. A price premium on B cannot be supported without some omitted advantage or constraint.
hint: Compare both terminal payoffs and intermediate services.

title: Cash timing restriction
prompt: At the start of a period a household holds 80 units of currency. Goods cost 2 each. Labor income arrives after purchases, and borrowing or paying on credit is impossible. Under P c≤M, what is maximum current consumption?
wrong: 80 units.
160 units.
It is unlimited if end-of-period labor income is large.
explanation: Only currency available before trading finances purchases: c≤80/2. Later income cannot relax this period’s timing restriction.
hint: Date the resources before dividing by the price.

title: Gross versus net settlement
prompt: A owes B 70 at noon and B owes A 60 at noon. Both obligations are legally eligible for simultaneous bilateral netting. What external settlement balance is required if neither has other obligations?
wrong: A needs 70 and B needs 60.
Both need 10.
No balance is needed because the obligations are simultaneous.
explanation: Netting cancels 60 in each direction, leaving A’s net liability of 10. Simultaneity alone would not erase the residual.
hint: Cancel only mutually offsetting obligations.

title: Payment versus credit instrument
prompt: A household uses a card that instructs a bank to transfer an existing deposit immediately, with no overdraft. In this stipulated arrangement, which object is the spendable monetary claim?
wrong: The plastic card itself.
A newly issued household bond on every purchase.
The merchant’s physical inventory.
explanation: The card is an instruction mechanism. The deposit is the claim being transferred; no new credit is supplied under the assumptions.
hint: Distinguish a payment instruction from the asset it moves.

title: Liquidity premium arithmetic
prompt: A riskless bond pays a net yield of 5% over a year. A liquid claim has the same risk and maturity but pays 3%. An investor is indifferent, and values liquidity additively in percentage points of return. What annual liquidity-service value rationalizes this choice?
wrong: 8 percentage points.
2 percent of the 3% yield.
Negative 2 percentage points.
explanation: Indifference requires 3% plus the liquidity service to equal 5%. This is an additive service valuation under the stated preference approximation.
hint: Equate total pecuniary and service returns.

title: Public liquidity under a pledgeability limit
prompt: A project costs 100 and pays 130 for certain. Only 60 of its payoff can be pledged to lenders; its owner has 25 in liquid wealth. Lenders require a zero interest rate on this certain pledgeable payoff. With no other funding source, what minimum additional liquid wealth permits financing?
wrong: Zero because total payoff exceeds cost.
explanation: Borrowing is capped at 60, so the owner must contribute 40. Existing liquid wealth is 25, leaving a 15 shortfall despite positive project surplus.
hint: Use pledgeable payoff, not total payoff, in the funding constraint.
skill: public liquidity under a pledgeability limit

title: Collateral haircut
prompt: A security has market value 200. A lender permits borrowing equal to (1−h) times collateral value, with haircut h=0.25. What is maximum borrowing?
explanation: The haircut excludes 25% of collateral value from loan capacity: 0.75×200=150.
hint: Translate the haircut into the fraction that can be borrowed.

title: A liquidity shortage without insolvency
prompt: A bank owes a withdrawal of 30 today, holds cash of 10, and has a certain asset payoff of 100 tomorrow against total liabilities of 80. Assets cannot be sold or pledged today. Which diagnosis follows?
correct: It is solvent on these undiscounted payoffs but cannot meet today’s withdrawal.
wrong: It is insolvent because cash is below the withdrawal.
It can pay today because tomorrow’s assets exceed total liabilities.
Its equity is necessarily negative 20.
explanation: Total assets of 110 exceed liabilities of 80, but only 10 is available today. The maturity restriction prevents using future solvency to settle today.
hint: Evaluate the timing constraint separately from net worth.

title: Token acceptance externality
prompt: A token has no redemption value. A buyer values holding it only because a future seller may accept it. Holding costs are positive and no seller is expected to accept it. Which choice is privately optimal?
correct: Do not pay a positive price to acquire the token.
wrong: Acquire it at any price because supply is finite.
Acquire it because every token is necessarily legal tender.
Acquire it because a zero redemption value guarantees appreciation.
explanation: With no expected exchange service or redemption payoff and positive holding cost, buying at a positive price yields negative value. Scarcity alone does not supply a benefit.
hint: List all stipulated sources of value.

title: Reserve transfer accounting
prompt: Bank A transfers 20 of reserves to Bank B to settle its customer’s deposit payment to B’s customer. Ignore fees and other entries. What happens to aggregate reserves and aggregate customer deposits across these two banks?
wrong: Both aggregates rise by 20.
Reserves fall by 20 while deposits are unchanged.
Deposits rise by 20 while reserves are unchanged.
explanation: A loses 20 of reserves and deposits; B gains 20 of each. The payment redistributes both stocks without creating either aggregate.
hint: Sum the paired balance-sheet entries across banks.

title: Transaction-balance optimization
prompt: A household spends T uniformly during a period and converts bonds to cash N times at fixed cost b each. Average cash is T/(2N); its opportunity cost is i per unit. Assume b, i and T are strictly positive. With continuous N>0, minimize bN+iT/(2N). How does optimal average cash change when b quadruples?
wrong: It quadruples.
It halves.
It stays unchanged.
explanation: The first-order condition gives N*=√(iT/(2b)) and average cash √(bT/(2i)). A fourfold conversion cost doubles desired average balances.
hint: Derive N before substituting into average cash.

title: Money demand opportunity cost
prompt: A deposit pays 2% while an otherwise comparable nonmonetary asset pays 6%. In a money-demand model where deposits supply liquidity and forgone interest is the only holding cost, what interest opportunity cost enters demand?
wrong: 6 percentage points.
2 percentage points.
8 percentage points.
explanation: The relevant sacrifice is the yield difference, 6%−2%, rather than either asset’s yield alone.
hint: Compare the return obtained with the return forgone.

title: Stable money demand and velocity
prompt: Real money demand is M/P=kY with constant k=0.25. Define income velocity as PY/M. What is velocity?
wrong: It equals the inflation rate.
explanation: Substituting M=0.25PY into PY/M gives 1/0.25=4. Constancy follows from the stipulated k, not an empirical claim.
hint: Invert the money-to-income ratio.

title: Conditional multiplier calculation
prompt: In a stylized steady balance sheet, currency C=cD and reserves R=rD, where c=0.2 and r=0.1. Define broad money M=C+D and base B=C+R. What is M/B?
explanation: M/B=(1+c)/(c+r)=1.2/0.3=4. This is an accounting ratio under fixed ratios, not a claim that lending is mechanically reserve constrained.
hint: Express both aggregates as multiples of deposits.

title: Loan origination entries
prompt: A bank grants a loan of 50 by crediting its borrower’s deposit account by 50. There are no fees, provisions or immediate payments. Which initial change occurs?
correct: Loans and deposits each rise by 50; equity is unchanged.
wrong: Reserves and equity each rise by 50.
Loans rise by 50 and deposits fall by 50.
Equity rises by 50 with no liability created.
explanation: The bank records a loan asset and an equal deposit liability. Creating the claim does not create bank equity or immediately alter reserves.
hint: Match the new asset to its financing entry.

title: Capital constraint on lending
prompt: A bank has equity 12 and risk-weighted assets 100. A capital rule requires equity/RWA≥10%. New loans carry unit risk weights; equity and all other assets stay fixed. What is its maximum additional lending?
explanation: Maximum RWA is 12/0.10=120, leaving 20 of headroom. This calculation assumes no retained earnings, capital issuance or risk-weight changes.
hint: Compute allowable total RWA before subtracting existing RWA.

title: Deposit outflow and funding replacement
prompt: A bank loses 10 of deposits and settles the outflow with 10 of reserves. It then borrows 10 in the interbank market, receiving reserves. Ignore costs. Relative to the initial balance sheet, what changed after both steps?
correct: Deposits are 10 lower and interbank borrowing is 10 higher; assets and equity return to their initial levels.
wrong: Equity is 10 lower.
Total assets permanently rise by 10.
Deposits return to their initial level.
explanation: Settlement reduces an asset and liability. Replacement borrowing restores reserves while substituting wholesale debt for deposit funding.
hint: Track the two transactions separately before netting them.

title: Run incentives and liquidation
prompt: A bank has one long asset worth 120 tomorrow but only 60 if liquidated today, and promises total deposits of 100. Early withdrawals are served first at par until cash runs out. Why can expectations of widespread early withdrawal encourage a depositor to withdraw early?
correct: Waiting may leave insufficient proceeds after others force liquidation and receive payment first.
wrong: The long asset is fundamentally worth less than deposits tomorrow.
Liquidation increases total asset value.
Sequential service guarantees every depositor payment regardless of withdrawals.
explanation: The asset covers deposits if held, yet liquidation destroys value and service priority exposes late withdrawers. This is a strategic liquidity mechanism, not initial fundamental insolvency.
hint: Compare payoffs to waiting when others withdraw.

title: Interest-sensitive money demand
prompt: Suppose real money demand is m=Y exp(−a s), where s is the yield spread in decimal units and a=5. At fixed Y, s rises by 0.02. What is the exact ratio of new to old money demand?
wrong: 0.90 exactly.
exp(0.1), approximately 1.105.
explanation: Taking the ratio cancels income and the initial spread. The exponent changes by −5×0.02=−0.1; a 10% decline is only a first-order approximation.
hint: Use the change in the exponent, with spreads measured in decimals.

title: Precautionary reserves
prompt: A bank chooses reserves R before uncertain net withdrawals W. Holding reserves has positive cost; shortfalls incur a penalty proportional to max(W−R,0). If the distribution of W shifts right by first-order stochastic dominance, what happens to optimal R for a unique interior optimum and unchanged costs?
wrong: It necessarily falls.
It is determined solely by last period’s withdrawals.
It remains fixed because expected withdrawal size cannot affect a bank.
explanation: The marginal benefit of an extra reserve unit is the penalty rate times Pr(W>R). A rightward shift weakly raises that benefit at each R, shifting the unique optimum weakly upward.
hint: Differentiate expected shortage cost using its tail probability.

title: Corridor arbitrage bounds
prompt: In a frictionless model all banks can deposit unlimited funds at the central bank at 2% and borrow unlimited funds there at 5%, with identical maturities and no stigma. Where can a competitive overnight unsecured bank rate lie if bank credit risk is zero?
wrong: Below 2% only.
Above 5% only.
Exactly 3.5% regardless of reserve supply.
explanation: Banks will not lend below an accessible deposit alternative or borrow above an accessible loan alternative. These bounds alone do not select an interior rate.
hint: Compare market lending and borrowing to the two outside options.

title: Reserve satiation
prompt: Banks are satiated in settlement reserves at the margin. In a frictionless model, extra reserves earn 3% and an overnight interbank loan is equally safe with identical maturity. What rate is consistent with indifference?
wrong: Zero necessarily.
Any rate because reserves are abundant.
explanation: After marginal liquidity services vanish, equal-risk arbitrage equates the market return to reserve remuneration. Abundance does not imply zero remuneration.
hint: Remove the marginal liquidity benefit but retain the asset yield.

title: Asset purchase from a nonbank
prompt: A central bank purchases a bond worth 40 from a nonbank investor through its commercial bank. Payment credits the investor’s deposit and the bank’s reserve account. Ignore valuation effects. What are the immediate bank changes?
correct: Reserves and deposit liabilities each rise by 40.
wrong: Loans and equity each rise by 40.
Reserves rise by 40 and deposits fall by 40.
The commercial bank’s bond holdings necessarily rise by 40.
explanation: The nonbank gives up the bond. The intermediary receives a reserve asset and owes the investor an equal deposit liability.
hint: Keep the seller’s balance sheet distinct from its bank’s.

title: Duration channel with segmented demand
prompt: Long bonds and overnight assets are imperfect substitutes because preferred-habitat investors have limited arbitrage capacity. Holding expected short rates fixed, a central-bank purchase reduces long-bond supply to private investors. If inverse demand slopes downward in bond quantity, what happens?
correct: Long-bond prices rise and yields fall.
wrong: Long-bond prices fall and yields rise.
Expected short rates must rise by assumption.
Bond prices cannot change unless coupon payments change.
explanation: Reduced available quantity raises the market-clearing price along downward-sloping demand. For fixed promised cash flows, a higher price implies a lower yield.
hint: Hold cash flows and expected short rates fixed and trace supply.

title: Term premium decomposition
prompt: In an additive approximation, the two-year yield equals the average expected one-year short rate over the two years plus a term premium. Expected short rates are 2% and 4%, and the premium is 0.5 percentage points. What is the two-year yield?
explanation: The expected-rate component is (2+4)/2=3%; adding the stated premium gives 3.5%. This uses the approximation supplied, not exact compounding.
hint: Average the two short rates before adding the premium.

title: Credit spread offset
prompt: A borrower’s loan rate equals the policy rate plus a spread. Policy falls from 4% to 3%, while the spread rises from 2 to 3.5 percentage points. What happens to the loan rate?
wrong: It falls by 1 percentage point.
It remains 6%.
It rises to 7.5%.
explanation: The 1.5-point spread increase more than offsets the one-point policy reduction, increasing the borrowing rate by 0.5 point.
hint: Calculate the all-in loan rate in each state.

title: Balance-sheet amplification
prompt: An entrepreneur may borrow at most θqK, with fixed collateral quantity K>0 and constant pledgeability θ>0. A policy contraction reduces collateral price q while the debt limit binds. What is the immediate financing effect, holding other resources fixed?
wrong: Borrowing capacity rises because collateral is cheaper.
Borrowing capacity is unchanged because K is fixed.
Equity necessarily rises by the fall in collateral value.
explanation: The binding debt limit depends on collateral value, not merely its physical quantity. A lower q reduces θqK and available external funding.
hint: Differentiate the collateral limit with respect to q.

title: Policy implementation versus stance
prompt: A central bank doubles reserves while leaving reserve remuneration and the expected policy-rate path unchanged. In a stipulated frictionless satiated-reserve model, reserves and short bills are perfect substitutes and there are no signaling effects. What follows for aggregate demand through this swap alone?
correct: No effect follows through relative returns or liquidity services in this model.
wrong: Demand necessarily doubles.
Inflation necessarily doubles immediately.
The short market rate must fall to zero.
explanation: The model removes scarcity, imperfect substitutability and signals, so exchanging equivalent assets creates no marginal incentive change. The conclusion is conditional on these exclusions.
hint: Identify which channels the assumptions have explicitly shut down.

title: Central-bank information signal
prompt: An announcement both cuts the policy rate and reveals the central bank’s previously private forecast of weak activity. Why is the observed equity-price response not a clean estimate of the effect of the rate cut alone?
correct: It combines the policy intervention with news about fundamentals.
wrong: Equity prices cannot respond to forecasts.
A rate cut is never a monetary-policy action.
A narrow announcement window mechanically removes information effects.
explanation: Even in a narrow window, the announcement can contain multiple shocks. News about weaker fundamentals may affect valuations independently of the rate decision.
hint: Separate the content of the announcement into distinct innovations.

title: Reserve averaging incentive
prompt: A bank must hold average reserves of 10 over two days and can shift holdings freely across days without settlement needs. It holds 14 on day one. What day-two holding exactly meets the average requirement?
explanation: The average requirement is (14+R₂)/2=10, hence R₂=6. This flexibility follows from averaging and the absence of a daily minimum.
hint: Translate an average requirement into a two-day total.

title: Predetermined nominal wage
prompt: A firm has labor demand L=(P/W)² with nominal wage W fixed at 10. Its output price P rises from 10 to 11. Under this stipulated demand schedule, what happens to employment?
wrong: It rises from 1 to 1.10.
It falls from 1 to 1/1.21.
It remains 1 because W is fixed.
explanation: The price increase lowers the real wage W/P. Substitution into the supplied schedule gives (11/10)²=1.21.
hint: A fixed nominal wage need not imply a fixed real wage.

title: State-dependent price adjustment
prompt: A firm may pay a fixed menu cost F to reset its price. The present value of the profit gain from resetting is G, calculated before paying F. It can otherwise keep its price and has no other adjustment consequence. When is resetting strictly optimal?
wrong: Whenever inflation is positive, regardless of G.
When G<F.
Only when every competitor resets simultaneously.
explanation: The net gain is G−F. The comparison creates a state-dependent inaction region rather than an exogenous reset probability.
hint: Compare the value gain to the fixed cost.

title: Relative-price dispersion
prompt: Two equally weighted firms charge prices 1 and 3. A uniform proportional doubling changes their prices to 2 and 6. Define dispersion as the variance of log price across firms. What happens to this dispersion?
wrong: It doubles.
It quadruples.
It becomes zero.
explanation: Doubling adds log 2 to each log price. Adding a common constant leaves variance unchanged, even though the nominal price level rises.
hint: Use the translation invariance of variance.

title: Inflation versus price-level restoration
prompt: A price index starts at 100 and unexpectedly reaches 104. In the next period, policy exactly restores the original price level of 100. What next-period inflation rate is required?
wrong: −4% exactly.
explanation: The required change is 100/104−1=−0.0384615. Reversing a percentage increase requires dividing by the new base.
hint: Use the current price level as the denominator.

title: Indexation and inflation persistence
prompt: Suppose inflation obeys πₜ=γπₜ₋₁+uₜ, with γ=0.6, and no other terms. A one-time shock sets π₀=2 percentage points above baseline; uₜ=0 for t≥1. What is π₂ relative to baseline?
wrong: 1.2 percentage points.
2 percentage points.
0.36 percentage points.
explanation: Two periods of decay give 2×0.6²=0.72. This persistence is imposed by indexation-like lag dependence in the specified reduced form.
hint: Apply the recurrence twice.

title: Inflation redistribution on nominal debt
prompt: A debtor must repay 110 nominal units next year. Expected price level at repayment was 100, but it is 110. Repayment is certain and the debt is not indexed. Relative to expectations, what happens to the real repayment?
correct: It falls from 1.1 to 1 unit of the consumption basket.
wrong: It rises from 1 to 1.1.
It stays 110 baskets.
It rises because nominal debt is fixed.
explanation: Real repayment is nominal repayment divided by the realized price level. Unexpected inflation reduces the real transfer to the creditor on this fixed nominal contract.
hint: Deflate the same nominal payment by each price level.

title: Inflation tax on existing currency
prompt: A household holds 100 units of noninterest-bearing currency through a rise in the price level from 1 to 1.25. It makes no transactions. What fraction of its initial purchasing power is lost?
wrong: Zero because currency units are unchanged.
explanation: Initial purchasing power is 100 and final purchasing power is 80. The loss as a fraction of the initial value is 20/100.
hint: Distinguish price inflation from the decline in its reciprocal.

title: Seigniorage and the tax base
prompt: In a stationary continuous-time illustration, real balances are m(π)=exp(−2π) and real seigniorage is s(π)=πm(π), with π≥0. What inflation rate maximizes this revenue?
wrong: Revenue rises without bound as π increases.
explanation: s′=exp(−2π)(1−2π), positive below 0.5 and negative above it. The tax base shrinks enough beyond that point to reduce revenue.
hint: Differentiate both the tax rate and its endogenous base.

title: Monetary neutrality counterexample
prompt: A one-period economy has preset nominal wages and demand-determined employment. A monetary expansion raises the goods price before wages can reset. Which assumption blocks a general inference of immediate real neutrality?
correct: The nominal wage cannot adjust with the goods price.
wrong: Money is measured in currency units.
The model contains a price index.
The monetary expansion is represented as a number.
explanation: Incomplete contemporaneous nominal adjustment changes the real wage and potentially employment. A units-of-account relabeling argument would require proportional adjustment of all relevant nominal contracts.
hint: Find the nominal contract whose real value changes.

title: Bayesian updating about inflation
prompt: An agent has a normal prior for inflation with mean 2 and variance 1. A signal equals inflation plus independent normal noise of variance 3 and has realized value 6. What is the posterior mean?
explanation: The signal weight is prior variance/(prior variance+noise variance)=1/4. The posterior mean is 2+(1/4)(6−2)=3.
hint: Weight the signal innovation by its precision relative to the prior.

title: Lower bound with a lending wedge
prompt: A policymaker can reduce its rate no lower than zero. Private borrowing costs equal that rate plus an exogenous 3-point spread. If the desired private nominal borrowing rate is 1%, can rate cuts alone attain it?
correct: No; the minimum private borrowing rate is 3%.
wrong: Yes, setting the policy rate to 1% does so.
Yes, setting the policy rate to zero gives a 1% loan rate.
No, because the minimum private borrowing rate is zero.
explanation: The spread creates a wedge between the constrained policy instrument and the rate affecting borrowers. A 1% loan rate would require a −2% policy rate here.
hint: Solve for the policy rate needed after subtracting the spread.
skill: lower bound with a lending wedge

title: Fiscal purchases with constrained households
prompt: In a static closed economy with fixed prices and idle capacity, Y=C+G, C=20+0.75(Y−T), and T is fixed. Ignore investment and imports. What is dY/dG?
explanation: Substitution gives 0.25Y=20−0.75T+G, so the multiplier is 1/0.25=4. The result relies on the supplied spending rule and no offsetting capacity or monetary response.
hint: Collect all Y terms before differentiating.

title: Targeting a bank-specific panic
prompt: A bank has sound assets that pay after a temporary withdrawal wave. A collateralized liquidity loan can bridge the timing gap without changing policy rates. What friction does that loan address directly?
correct: The mismatch between immediate withdrawals and later asset payoffs.
wrong: A permanent negative asset value relative to liabilities in every state.
The absence of any profitable long-term projects in the economy.
The economy’s long-run population growth rate.
explanation: The loan provides settlement resources at the time they are needed. Solvency assumptions matter because bridging time does not itself repair a fundamental asset shortfall.
hint: Match the instrument’s maturity to the stated shortage.

title: Collateral eligibility and policy access
prompt: A central bank lends only against eligible bonds. Two otherwise identical solvent banks need liquidity; A owns eligible bonds and B owns only ineligible loans that cannot be sold. There is no interbank market. What follows?
correct: Only A can use the facility under the stated rules.
wrong: Both can borrow because solvency automatically overrides eligibility.
Neither can borrow because central-bank lending requires insolvency.
B can borrow by relabeling its loans as reserves.
explanation: Eligibility is a separate access constraint from solvency. Without asset sales or intermediated borrowing, B cannot route its assets into the facility.
hint: Check the actual constraint on facility access.

title: Commitment backed by a reputational loss
prompt: A policymaker gains 3 today by breaking a promise. Breaking it causes a loss of 1 each period forever beginning next period. With discount factor β=0.8, is keeping the promise incentive compatible under this punishment?
correct: Yes; the discounted loss is 4, exceeding the gain of 3.
wrong: No; the discounted loss is only 0.8.
No; future losses cannot affect current incentives.
Yes; the discounted loss is 5 because it starts today.
explanation: The punishment has value β/(1−β)=0.8/0.2=4. Comparing 4 with the immediate gain of 3 supports compliance under the specified repeated-game strategy.
hint: Date the first punishment period before summing the geometric series.
skill: commitment backed by a reputational loss

title: Instrument uncertainty
prompt: A policymaker chooses action a before learning its effectiveness b. The target is y=1 and y=ba. It minimizes E[(ba−1)²], with E[b]=1 and Var(b)=1. What is optimal a?
explanation: The first-order condition is aE[b²]=E[b]. Since E[b²]=Var(b)+E[b]²=2, a=1/2. This result is specific to multiplicative instrument uncertainty and quadratic loss.
hint: Expand expected squared loss and retain the second moment of b.

title: Distributional effects of refinancing
prompt: Two borrowers have identical debt principal. A policy cut immediately reduces A’s adjustable loan rate but B’s fixed rate cannot reset and refinancing is prohibited. Holding income and prices fixed, whose current interest payment falls?
wrong: Both fall equally.
Only B’s.
Neither can change because debt principal is fixed.
explanation: Contractual repricing determines immediate cash-flow exposure. Equal principal does not make the current interest burden equally responsive.
hint: Identify which contract passes the new rate into current payments.

title: Aggregate demand with offsetting balance-sheet effects
prompt: A rate cut raises constrained borrowers’ disposable cash flow by 10 and lowers savers’ interest income by 10. Their marginal propensities to consume are 0.9 and 0.2 respectively; ignore other effects. What is the net consumption change?
wrong: Zero.
An increase of 11.
A decrease of 7.
explanation: Borrowers add 0.9×10=9 to spending while savers reduce it by 0.2×10=2. The net is 7 despite zero aggregate income transfer.
hint: Apply each group’s propensity before aggregating.
skill: aggregate demand with offsetting balance-sheet effects

title: Price-level history dependence
prompt: A target price path rises from 100 to 102 to 104.04. Actual prices at the middle date are 103. A policy restores the target path exactly at the last date. What final-period inflation is required?
explanation: Restoring the target path requires 104.04/103−1≈0.010097. Past overshooting reduces the growth required to reach the specified future level.
hint: Use the future target level and the actual inherited level.

title: Two targets and instrument rank
prompt: Two policy instruments a and b affect inflation and a credit gap by Δπ=a+b and Δc=2a+2b. Can the policymaker independently choose any pair (Δπ,Δc)?
wrong: Yes, because there are two named instruments.
Yes, because both coefficients are positive.
No; neither variable can be changed at all.
explanation: The instrument-effect columns are identical, so the mapping has rank one. Two labels do not provide two independent directions of control.
hint: Check whether the two target equations are independent.

title: Policy reaction versus shock
prompt: A central bank raises its rate whenever its private forecast of demand rises. A researcher regresses later output on the observed rate without controlling for that forecast. Why need the coefficient not measure a contractionary policy effect?
correct: The rate also reflects demand news that independently raises output.
wrong: Interest rates cannot be explanatory variables.
A negative causal policy effect requires a negative raw correlation.
A large sample automatically removes forecast-driven endogeneity.
explanation: Systematic responses to demand news create correlation between the rate and omitted output determinants. Identification requires isolating an exogenous policy component.
hint: Distinguish a policy innovation from an endogenous policy response.

title: Narrative identification exclusion
prompt: A narrative instrument records rate changes described as responses to inflation concerns. Some concerns reflect private forecasts of a coming supply shock that directly lowers output. Which instrumental-variable condition is threatened?
correct: Instrument exogeneity: orthogonality to structural output disturbances.
wrong: The requirement that every instrument be normally distributed.
The requirement that the instrument have the same units as output.
The requirement that the first-stage coefficient equal one.
explanation: The recorded motivation can encode supply news with its own output effect, correlating the instrument with structural output disturbances. This is a common-cause exogeneity problem; the instrument need not itself cause a separate direct effect on output. Narrative labeling alone does not establish a valid instrument.
hint: Ask whether the information used to construct the instrument also predicts nonpolicy output disturbances.

title: High-frequency surprise scaling
prompt: An announcement-window instrument moves the two-year yield by 0.20 percentage points in the first stage and output by −0.10% in the reduced form, using consistent event weighting. In a just-identified linear IV ratio, what is the output effect per one-percentage-point yield increase?
explanation: The Wald ratio is −0.10/0.20=−0.5 percent output per percentage point of yield. Its causal interpretation still depends on relevance and exclusion.
hint: Divide the reduced-form response by the first-stage response.

title: Weak first stage
prompt: An instrument is plausibly exogenous but has population covariance zero with the policy innovation. Can it identify that innovation’s causal coefficient in a just-identified linear IV model?
wrong: Yes; exogeneity alone is sufficient.
Yes; setting the denominator of the IV ratio to zero identifies a zero effect.
Yes; increasing sample size creates population relevance.
explanation: The moment cannot separate the coefficient if the instrument has no covariance with the treatment. A larger sample does not change a zero population first stage.
hint: Inspect the denominator of the population IV expression.

title: Recursive ordering restriction
prompt: A quarterly structural VAR orders output before the policy rate in a recursive identification. Output can respond to its own shock contemporaneously, but is restricted not to respond within the quarter to a policy shock. Which claim is imposed rather than learned from the covariance matrix alone?
correct: The absence of a within-quarter output response to the policy shock.
wrong: That lagged output is observable.
That the reduced-form residual covariance can be estimated.
That the sample contains quarters.
explanation: The recursive impact restriction selects a structural decomposition of correlated residuals. Reduced-form covariances do not by themselves establish the required timing exclusion.
hint: Locate the zero restriction that gives the ordering its economic content.

title: Local-projection horizon meaning
prompt: A researcher estimates y(t+h)−y(t−1)=αh+βh εt+controls+error, where y is log output and εt is a valid policy shock. What does βh describe?
correct: The effect on cumulative log-output growth from t−1 through t+h per unit shock.
wrong: The sum of output levels from t through t+h.
Only the one-period growth rate between t+h−1 and t+h for every h.
The contemporaneous policy reaction to output at t+h.
explanation: The dependent variable is a log-level difference spanning the full interval. It is not the sum of level responses or a terminal one-period growth rate.
hint: Read the estimand directly from the left-hand-side transformation.

title: Post-treatment credit control
prompt: A valid policy shock affects output partly by changing bank credit. A regression of output on that shock adds contemporaneous credit, measured after the shock, as a control. Why can its coefficient fail to estimate the total policy effect?
correct: The control blocks part of the transmission pathway and may introduce further selection bias.
wrong: Adding controls always recovers the total effect more precisely.
Credit cannot respond to monetary policy by definition.
A valid shock becomes mechanically larger after controlling for credit.
explanation: Conditioning on a mediator removes the path through that mediator; with additional causes of credit and output, it can also induce bias. Random or exogenous treatment does not make post-treatment adjustment harmless.
hint: Draw the path from the shock through credit to output.

title: Anticipated announcements
prompt: A policy increase is fully anticipated one day before its official announcement. A researcher measures only the yield change in a narrow window on announcement day. What can a zero measured surprise establish?
correct: There was no measured new yield news in that window; it does not establish that the policy change had no effect.
wrong: The anticipated increase had no effect at any earlier date.
The policy rate did not change.
The central bank had no reason for changing policy.
explanation: Expected changes can already be incorporated in prices. Announcement-day surprise measures innovations relative to expectations, not the entire effect of anticipated policy.
hint: Separate the date news arrives from the implementation or announcement date.

title: Cumulative response accounting
prompt: A valid shock causes quarterly output-level deviations of −1, −2 and −1 units over three quarters, and zero otherwise. What is the cumulative output loss over these quarters, measured in output-unit quarters?
wrong: 2 output-unit quarters.
1 output-unit quarter.
A permanent loss of 4 units every quarter thereafter.
explanation: Summing deviations gives −4; the loss magnitude is 4. This area under a level-response path is distinct from its peak or long-run effect.
hint: Sum flow deviations over their durations.

title: Policy evaluation beyond point estimates
prompt: Two admissible structural models fit the available policy-shock responses equally well. They imply opposite welfare rankings of two untried policy rules because of different unobserved distortion parameters. What conclusion is warranted?
correct: The fitted responses alone do not identify the welfare ranking; additional restrictions or evidence are needed.
wrong: The rule with the larger measured output response must maximize welfare.
Equal fit proves that all welfare parameters are identified.
One may average the rankings and call the result identified.
explanation: Observational equivalence on these responses leaves welfare-relevant structure unresolved. Rule evaluation can require more information than estimating a particular shock response.
hint: Ask which welfare parameters are pinned down by the observed moments.
